Power series¶

The term power series describes a series whose terms contain different powers of the variable xxx. The kkkthe term in a power series consists of some coefficient ckc_kck​ and the kkkth power of xxx:

Pn(x)=∑k=0nckxk=c0+c1x+c2x2+c3x3+⋯+cnxn.P_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n c_k x^k = c_0 + c_1x + c_2x^2 + c_3x^3 % + c_4x^4 + c_5x^5 + \cdots + c_nx^n.Pn​(x)=k=0∑n​ck​xk=c0​+c1​x+c2​x2+c3​x3+⋯+cn​xn.
(56)

The math expression we obtain in this way is a polynomial of degree nnn in xxx, which we denote Pn(x)P_n(x)Pn​(x). Depending on the choice of the coefficients (c0,c1,c2,c3,…,cn)(c_0, c_1, c_2, c_3, \ldots, c_n)(c0​,c1​,c2​,c3​,…,cn​) we can make the polynomial function Pn(x)P_n(x)Pn​(x) approximate some other function f:R→Rf : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}f:R→R. To find such approximations, we need some way to choose the coefficients ckc_kck​ of the power series, so that the resulting polynomial approximates the function: Pn(x)≈f(x)P_n(x) \approx f(x)Pn​(x)≈f(x).

Taylor series¶

The Taylor series approximation to the function f(x)f(x)f(x) is a power series whose coefficients ckc_kck​ are computed by evaluating the kkkth derivative of the function f(x)f(x)f(x) at x=0x=0x=0, which we denote f(k)(0)f^{(k)}(0)f(k)(0). Specifically, the kkkth coefficient in the Taylor series approximation for the function f(x)f(x)f(x) is ck=f(k)(0)k!c_k = \frac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}ck​=k!f(k)(0)​, where k!k!k! is the factorial function.

The finite Taylor series with nnn terms produces the following approximation:

f(x)≈f(0)+f′ ⁣(0)x+f′′(0)2!x2+⋯+f(n)(0)n!xn=∑k=0nf(k)(0)k!xk.\begin{align*} f(x) &\approx f(0) +f^{\prime\!}(0)x +\tfrac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2 % +\tfrac{f^{(3)}(0)}{3!}x^3 + \cdots +\tfrac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}x^n \\ % +\tfrac{f^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)}{3!}x^3 % +\tfrac{f^{(4)}(0)}{4!}x^4 + \cdots \\ &= \sum_{k=0}^n \tfrac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}x^k. \end{align*}f(x)​≈f(0)+f′(0)x+2!f′′(0)​x2+⋯+n!f(n)(0)​xn=k=0∑n​k!f(k)(0)​xk.​
(57)

In the limit as nnn goes to infinity, the Taylor series approximation becomes exactly equal to the function f(x)f(x)f(x):

f(x)=f(0)+f′ ⁣(0)x+f′′(0)2!x2+f(3)(0)3!x3+⋯=∑k=0∞f(k)(0)k!xk.\begin{align*} f(x) &= f(0) + f^{\prime\!}(0)x + \tfrac{f^{\prime\prime}(0)}{2!}x^2 + \tfrac{f^{(3)}(0)}{3!}x^3 + \cdots \\ &= \sum_{k=0}^\infty \tfrac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}x^k. \end{align*}f(x)​=f(0)+f′(0)x+2!f′′(0)​x2+3!f(3)(0)​x3+⋯=k=0∑∞​k!f(k)(0)​xk.​
(58)

Using this formula and your knowledge of derivative formulas, you can compute the Taylor series of any function f(x)f(x)f(x). For example, let’s find the Taylor series of the function f(x)=exf(x) = e^xf(x)=ex at x=0x=0x=0. The first derivative of f(x)=exf(x) = e^xf(x)=ex is f′ ⁣(x)=exf^{\prime\!}(x) = e^xf′(x)=ex. The second derivative of f(x)=exf(x) = e^xf(x)=ex is f′′ ⁣(x)=exf^{\prime\prime\!}(x) = e^xf′′(x)=ex. In fact, all the derivatives of f(x)f(x)f(x) will be exe^xex because the derivative of exe^xex is equal to exe^xex. The kkkth coefficient in the power series of f(x)=exf(x)=e^xf(x)=ex at the point x=0x=0x=0 is equal to the value of the kkkth derivative of f(x)f(x)f(x) evaluated at x=0x=0x=0 divided by k!k!k!. In the case of f(x)=exf(x) = e^xf(x)=ex, we have f(k)(0)=e0=1f^{(k)}(0) = e^0 = 1f(k)(0)=e0=1. The coefficient of the kkkth term is ck=f(k)(0)k!=1k!c_k = \tfrac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!} = \tfrac{1}{k!}ck​=k!f(k)(0)​=k!1​, so the Taylor series of f(x)=exf(x) = e^xf(x)=ex is

ex=∑k=0∞1k!xk=1+x+x22+x33!+x44!+x55!+x66!+x77!+⋯e^x = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \tfrac{1}{k!}x^k = 1 + x + \tfrac{x^2}{2} + \tfrac{x^3}{3!} + \tfrac{x^4}{4!} + \tfrac{x^5}{5!} + \tfrac{x^6}{6!} + \tfrac{x^7}{7!} + \cdotsex=k=0∑∞​k!1​xk=1+x+2x2​+3!x3​+4!x4​+5!x5​+6!x6​+7!x7​+⋯
(59)

Taylor series are a powerful computational tool for approximating functions. As we compute more terms from the above series, the polynomial approximation to the function f(x)=exf(x)=e^xf(x)=ex becomes more accurate.

Obtaining Taylor series using SymPy¶

The SymPy function series is a convenient way to obtain the series of any function fun. Calling sp.series(fun,var,x0,n) will show you the series expansion of expr near var=x0 including all powers of var less than n.

import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")

sp.series(1/(1-x), x, x0=0, n=8)
Loading...
sp.series(1/(1+x), x, x0=0, n=8)
Loading...
sp.series(sp.E**x, x, x0=0, n=7)
Loading...
sp.series(sp.sin(x), x, x0=0, n=9)
Loading...
sp.series(sp.cos(x), x, x0=0, n=8)
Loading...
sp.series(sp.ln(x+1), x, x0=0, n=6)
Loading...

Applications of series¶

Series allow us to compute numbers like eee, π\piπ, ln⁡(2)\ln(2)ln(2), etc. Taylor series allow us to approximate functions exe^xex, sin⁡(x)\sin(x)sin(x), cos⁡(x)\cos(x)cos(x), etc.

The Taylor series representation for the function f(x)f(x)f(x) provides an easy way to compute its integral function F0(x)=∫0xf(u) duF_0(x) = \int_0^x f(u)\,duF0​(x)=∫0x​f(u)du. The Taylor series f(x)=∑k=0∞ckxkf(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k x^kf(x)=∑k=0∞​ck​xk consists only of polynomial terms of the form ckxkc_k x^kck​xk. To compute the integral function F0F_0F0​, we can compute the integral of each term, which is ∫ckxk dx=ckk+1xk+1\int c_k x^k \,dx = \frac{c_k}{k+1}x^{k+1}∫ck​xkdx=k+1ck​​xk+1. This means the Taylor series of the integral function is F0(x)=∑k=0∞ckk+1xk+1+CF_0(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{c_k}{k+1}x^{k+1} + CF0​(x)=∑k=0∞​k+1ck​​xk+1+C.
